title: Issuance of Orders under Internal Security Act (ISA) against two self-radicalised Singaporean youths, and updates on ISA Orders

reading.body:
This is a case of online radicalisation that was detected and acted on by a state security apparatus rather than a case of an AI system failing. The reporting describes two teenagers who consumed extremist material online, one pledging allegiance to the Islamic State and one drawing on far-right material, and who were handled under the Internal Security Act. The failure described is one of influence and intent, not of a model or product.

The relevant point for a catalogue of deployed systems is that the radicalisation is described as having happened online, and that the 17-year-old was an online contact of a person detained the previous December. The reports do not identify any platform, algorithm, recommendation system or AI tool as the mechanism, so no specific system can be named here. What would have caught it earlier is not established by the facts given, beyond the minister's general call for families and friends to report suspected radicalisation.

The 17-year-old's plans were stopped because he failed to obtain a gun, which is a material obstacle rather than a detection. It is not established that any automated system flagged either teenager, and the reports do not state how the authorities became aware of them. A detention or restriction order under the ISA is an executive action, not a criminal conviction, and the reporting does not establish intent beyond what the authorities have stated.

reports.title: Singaporean Islamic State supporter the first female youth caught under ISA; another teen detained for far-right extremism
Issuance of Orders under Internal Security Act (ISA) against two self-radicalised Singaporean youths, and updates on ISA Orders

summary:
Singapore has dealt with two more self-radicalised teenagers under the Internal Security Act. A 15-year-old girl who supported the Islamic State is the first female youth and second-youngest person to face such action, receiving a restriction order. She pledged allegiance to the group online, posted propaganda, and hoped to marry a fighter in Syria. A 17-year-old boy was detained after planning attacks on five mosques, aiming to kill at least 100 people and livestream the violence. He was influenced by far-right material and identified as an "East Asian Supremacist."

The 17-year-old was an online contact of Nick Lee Xing Qiu, who was detained last December. He failed to obtain a gun, which stopped his plans. Since 2015, 17 youths aged 20 and below have been handled under the ISA, all self-radicalised online. The Home Affairs Minister urged families and friends to report suspected radicalisation, noting many cases can be rehabilitated.
